column1: How does propeller thrust scale with angular velocity (ω) in the low subsonic regime for a fixed-pitch propeller?
column2: Thrust scales approximately with the square of angular velocity: T ∝ ω². Doubling RPM quadruples thrust.

column1: In the canonical X-frame quadcopter motor configuration, how are the four motors' spin directions arranged to cancel net yaw torque?
column2: Motors 1 and 3 (front-right, rear-left) spin clockwise; motors 2 and 4 (front-left, rear-right) spin counterclockwise (viewed from above), canceling reaction torque when all motors run at equal speed.

column1: What is the nominal voltage, full-charge voltage, and critical low-voltage cutoff danger zone for a single LiPo cell?
column2: Full charge: 4.20V; nominal plateau: 3.7V; below ~3.5V the voltage collapses steeply and the cell risks permanent damage.

column1: Why is the flat discharge curve of LiPo cells considered a double-edged property for FPV pilots?
column2: It provides consistent motor performance across most of the pack's capacity, but gives almost no early warning before sudden voltage collapse, leading pilots who fly by feel to over-discharge and damage packs.

column1: Calculate the theoretical continuous discharge current for a 1500 mAh pack rated at 100C.
column2: 150 A (0.1 Ah of capacity scaled: 1.5 Ah × 100C = 150 A). Note: real packs rarely achieve their marketed C-rating.

column1: What physically happens during LiPo thermal runaway, and why must a puffed pack never be recharged?
column2: Excessive current demand heats the electrolyte, raising internal resistance; the separator melts, cathode/anode contact directly, and an exothermic self-sustaining reaction occurs. A puffed pack has already decomposed electrolyte (gas = lithium fluoride + organic carbonates) with a compromised separator, making recharging dangerous.

column1: Why are multirotor aircraft fundamentally different from fixed-wing aircraft in terms of open-loop stability?
column2: Multirotors are fundamentally unstable in open-loop operation (no inherent aerodynamic stability like swept wings/tail surfaces), so the slightest disturbance causes rapid divergence unless corrected by closed-loop control within tens of milliseconds.

column1: What are the typical control loop frequencies for the gyroscope-based PID controller versus the accelerometer/barometer fusion stage?
column2: Gyroscope PID loop: 4 kHz to 8 kHz. Accelerometer/barometer fusion: 500 Hz to 1 kHz (lower bandwidth).

column1: In a flight controller's sensor fusion scheme, what distinct role does each sensor play (gyroscope, accelerometer, barometer)?
column2: Gyroscope: high-frequency, low-drift angular rate. Accelerometer: corrects gyro integration drift over seconds using gravity reference (but noisy under vibration/maneuvers). Barometer: provides altitude reference, stabilizing altitude hold when GPS is unavailable.

column1: What are the three components of a PID controller and their individual functions in flight stabilization?
column2: Proportional: scales correction directly with instantaneous error. Integral: accumulates error over time to eliminate steady-state offset. Derivative: responds to rate of error change to dampen oscillation/overshoot.

column1: Why does the human vestibulo-ocular reflex impose a strict latency requirement on FPV video transmission?
column2: The VOR expects visual feedback within ~50 ms to maintain spatial orientation; exceeding this threshold causes dissociation between control input and observed response, degrading flight from intuitive control to error-prone prediction.

column1: What is the core philosophical difference between analog and digital FPV video transmission when handling radio interference?
column2: Analog degrades gracefully—signal corruption appears as progressive noise, preserving temporal consistency. Digital requires error-free packet reception; failed packets cause decoder stalls and freeze-frame artifacts (catastrophic failure vs. continuous degradation).
